query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating approximately 1-3 wt% of Y2O3 into the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix enables a dual-function improvement: the Y2O3 particles act as grain boundary pinning agents at room temperature to reduce wear and, at elevated temperatures, catalyze the formation of a stable, lubricious oxide tribolayer that maintains low friction and wear rates from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Baseline CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy exhibiting acceptable sliding performance at room temperature but degrading at high temperatures due to oxidative wear and phase instability.
generation.intervention: Introduce 1-3 wt% Y2O3 into the CoCrFeNi alloy.
generation.conditions: Sliding contact under constant normal load in an oxidizing environment, with test temperatures set at room temperature, 400 °C, 600 °C, and 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Finely dispersed Y2O3 particles within the CoCrFeNi matrix.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures, the Y2O3 particles act as grain boundary pinning agents to restrict undesirable grain growth and enhance wear resistance. At higher temperatures, they facilitate the formation of a protective and lubricious oxide tribolayer that mitigates adhesive and oxidative wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Y2O3-modified CoCrFeNi alloy will exhibit a consistently lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate across the full temperature range compared to the unmodified alloy.
generation.baseline: Unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy with temperature-dependent degradation in tribological performance.
generation.boundary: Operates in a sliding contact regime from room temperature to 800 °C under constant mechanical load in an oxidizing atmosphere.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal concentration of Y2O3 and the precise characteristics of the resultant tribolayer, especially at intermediate temperatures, require empirical determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of specimens: one set of baseline CoCrFeNi alloy samples and one set with 1-3 wt% Y2O3 addition. Subject both groups to controlled sliding wear tests at room temperature, 400 °C, 600 °C, and 800 °C under identical normal loads and in an oxidizing environment.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (COF) across temperature levels
Surface characterization (e.g., SEM/EDS) for the formation and stability of the oxide tribolayer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the Y2O3-modified specimens do not show a significant and consistent improvement in lower friction coefficients and reduced wear rates compared to the baseline across all temperatures or if the expected lubricious oxide tribolayer is not observed at elevated temperatures.

cited_evidence.text: Thus, if cooperative heterostructures capable of releasing frictional stress in stages are configured in the alloy, it is expected to suppress the sliding-induced deformation. In contrast, upon wear at high temperatures (≥600 °C), the wear behavior of the material becomes quite complex, stemming from the prevalence of surface adhesion and tribo-oxidation at the friction interface [,]. High-temperature sliding tends to soften the metallic surface that endows the near-surface material susceptible to chemical instability caused by counterbody materials or environmental oxygen, triggering severe delamination wear and composition segregation at the friction interface that exacerbates wear [,]. Materials become more dependent on tribochemical protection upon high-temperature wear due to deterioration in stiffness [,]. Tribo-oxidation may promote the formation of a protective oxide layer (glaze layer) consisting of various nanocrystalline (NC) oxides on the worn surface, which assists in enhancing the friction interface while providing solid lubrication [,,]. If the worn surface is replaced by a glaze layer as tribo-oxidation accumulates, a gentle wear scenario can be achieved. Neverthele

AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

AbstractA novel metal matrix composite CrMnFeCoNi with Y2O3 as reinforcement phase was designed and manufactured by mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering. After sintering at 900 °C for 5 min, the microstructure consisted of a FCC matrix and Y2O3 nanoparticles. The addition of 0.25 wt % Y2O3 increased the room temperature tensile strength of the CrMnFeCoNi base from 868 MPa to 1001 MPa, while the mechanical properties of the addition of 0.5 wt % Y2O3 composite decreased. In the meantime, the addition of Y2O3 had no significant influence on the coefficient of friction, while the addition of 0.25 wt % Y2O3 composite shows excellent wear-resistance.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, mechanical alloying, metal-matrix composites, Y2O3 nanoparticles, mechanical properties, tribological properties

HEA are a class of materials that contain 5–13 principal elements in near-equiatomic proportions; they have attracted a wide range of interesting research due to their excellent mechanical properties []. In recent years, a variety of HEA were reported publicly in the literature [,,,,]. Among them, AlCoCrFeNi HEA composed of a single BCC solid solution phase shows excellent corrosion resistance and has great potential for surface coating applications [,,,,,]. However, an insufficient high temperature wear-resistance of AlCoCrFeNi HEA greatly limits their practical applications at elevated temperatures (above 800 °C). According to the principle of dispersion strength, the strength and hardness of the simple solid solution phases could be improved further by the precipitated intermetallic compound phases. From the perspective of the dispersion strengthening mechanism, WC, TiC ceramic particles are commonly used as reinforcement phases in high-entropy alloys [,,]. These granular-shaped precipitates can improve the microhardness and wear resistance of the coating. frame.system: A CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix used in sliding contact applications, initially unmodified and exhibiting temperature-dependent friction and wear behavior.
frame.goal: Achieve and maintain a consistently low coefficient of friction and wear rate over a wide temperature range (room temperature to 800 °C).
frame.limitation: The material’s tribological performance degrades at high temperatures, making it difficult to maintain low friction and wear uniformly from room temperature through 800 °C.

frame.regime: Sliding contact under mechanical load in an oxidizing environment (typical of ambient to high-temperature conditions, specifically room temperature up to 800 °C), where both mechanical stress and temperature-induced oxidative reactions are at play.
prior_attempts: Use of the baseline CoCrFeNi matrix without modification has shown acceptable tribological behavior at room temperature but has failed to sustain low friction and wear at elevated temperatures, likely due to oxidation and phase instability.

Prior studies (as inferred from literature before the cutoff) on high-entropy alloys indicate that without surface or compositional modifications, the formation of detrimental oxides and loss of microstructural stability lead to increased wear and friction.
frame.understanding: The intervention should enable a mechanism that is active and self-adapting over the temperature range. At lower temperatures, the added phase should provide solid lubrication and hinder wear, while at high temperatures, it must promote the formation of a protective, lubricious oxide or tribo-film that mitigates friction and wear despite the changing environmental conditions.
frame.proposal: One hypothesis is that incorporating a well-dispersed minor addition (on the order of a few weight percent) of a high-temperature stable dispersoid such as Y2O3 into the CoCrFeNi matrix can serve as a single intervention to overcome the temperature-dependent tribological limitations. The Y2O3 particles are expected to act as a grain boundary pinning agent at room temperature, enhancing wear resistance, and at high temperatures, they should facilitate the formation of a stable, lubricious oxide tribolayer that minimizes friction. This dual-action mechanism would allow for consistent tribological performance over the entire temperature range. Relevant test conditions would include sliding tests conducted at ambient conditions as well as at 400 °C, 600 °C, and 800 °C, under the same applied loads and in an oxidizing environment. Prior evidence in related systems suggests that rare-earth oxides can stabilize microstructures and promote beneficial tribo-layer formation in high-temperature sliding environments. A controlled falsification experiment would involve preparing two sample sets—one with the Y2O3 dispersoid addition and one baseline CoCrFeNi—and subjecting them to identical sliding wear tests over the full temperature range. A failure of the hypothesis would be indicated if the Y2O3-modified samples either exhibit no significant improvement or degrade more rapidly in tribological performance compared to the baseline.
